included.title: Auto-Blend Layers: blend a layer the canvas crops to all-overlap (#5745)
included.body:
Fixes storytold/PhotoCraft#5745 (the all-black mask). Narrowed per review; the other behaviour changes are now #7395, #7396 and #7397.

**Cause:** in `panorama::seam_labels`, an image whose coverage lies wholly over the earlier images (`nn == no`) was skipped, so the earlier images kept every cell. In #5745, Auto-Align moves the second photo partly off the canvas. Cropped to the canvas, it's all overlap, so it got an all-black mask and the picture didn't change.

**Fix:** for such an image, its side of the seam is the one it lies towards from the composite's centre. An image centred on the composite (or covering the same cells) has no side and is still skipped, as before.

**Tests:**
- `panorama::tests::an_image_wholly_inside_the_composite_still_gets_its_side` (algo): the right-hand image gets one run on its side; the centred and same-cells cases keep the old result.
- `align_cmds::tests::auto_blend_panorama_of_a_layer_the_canvas_crops_to_all_overlap` (engine): the top layer hangs off the canvas and now shows on its side within the canvas.
- `cargo test -p photocraft-algo --lib an_image_wholly_inside` and `cargo test -p photocraft-engine --lib align_cmds::tests::auto_blend`: all pass.

included.head: 27466a8e5851b72eb47d82ae6d1b56525f2a7bdf
included.title: Move tool: ΔX/ΔY readout beside the pointer while dragging (#5727)
included.body:
Fixes #5727.

### What was wrong

The report says the Move tool used to show the same "how far I've moved it" tooltip as Ctrl+T, and doesn't in 0.9.0. In the code, no release (0.6.0 through 0.9.0, and `main`) ever drew a readout for a plain Move-tool drag. The only ΔX/ΔY readout is Free Transform's (`transform_tool::live_readout`, `Hit::Inside`). The Move tool reaches it only when a drag starts on one of its transform-control handles or the rotation band, which opens a Free Transform session. A drag *inside* the box, or with Show Transform Controls off, is an ordinary Move drag and showed nothing. So the reporter most likely saw it through Free Transform. Either way, Photoshop shows ΔX/ΔY for an ordinary Move drag, and PhotoCraft didn't.

### The change

- `move_ui::offset_readout`: the ΔX/ΔY strings for the Move drag in progress. It uses the same whole-pixel offset (`drag_offset`) that the live preview shows and the release commits through `layer.translate`. It returns `None` until the pointer has moved, so a click shows nothing.
- `canvas::draw_drag_preview` draws it at the pointer (`"move-readout"`), before the early return for selected-pixel drags, so it shows both when dragging a layer and when dragging selected pixels.
- It goes through `draw_value_readout`, so **Preferences › Tools › Show Transformation Values** hides it, like the marquee, crop and Free Transform readouts. Same `ΔX:`/`ΔY:` labels and `N px` format as Free Transform's offset readout.

### Test

`move_ui::tests::a_move_drag_reads_out_the_offset_it_will_commit`: no readout before the drag or right after the press; a drag to (+10.4, −3.2) reads `10 px` / `-3 px`, the offset the release commits; and nothing after the release.

### Not verified

Nothing was built or run locally (only `rustfmt --check`), and I took no screenshot. CI is the first compile and test run.

included.head: dcc824d477da5795142b38ac419651e8e0ac75fb
included.title: PSD: PSB foreign-order long-key blocks keep 8-byte length in little-endian TIFFs (#5599)
included.body:
Fixes part of #5599 (finding 2: PSB long-key length bug in the TIFF writer).

When a large-document (PSB) TIFF was saved back as little-endian, `crates/psd/src/tiff.rs` checked the byte-reversed key to decide the length size. The reversed key never matches the list of keys that get 8-byte lengths, so the length was read as 4 bytes and every block after it was corrupted. It now uses the key as stored, the same way the block writer does.

- Adds regression test `psb_foreign_order_long_key_block_keeps_its_8_byte_length`.
- `cargo test` and `cargo clippy -D warnings` pass for `photocraft-psd`.

included.head: 769cd2f725ce805ea82108d2b0a8e516d922b0de
included.title: Warp: apply a large layer's warp in the background, with progress and Esc to cancel (#1015)
included.body:
Part of #1015, as proposed in https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/issues/1015#issuecomment-6170728316. It's the Warp counterpart of #4218.

### Problem

Committing Edit › Transform › Warp ran on the UI thread, with no progress and no cancel. On an 8000 × 6000 layer the window froze for 6.9 s (Arc) and 9.3 s (Flag).

Timing the steps of a Flag warp showed where that time goes. The mesh warp itself (`warp_triangles`) took 1.3 s. Writing its tiles took 0.5 s (since #6800, each worker encodes its own tiles). Then two serial whole-layer passes in `warp_layer` took most of the rest:

- `surf.convert(…)` re-encoded every tile into the format the layer already had: **2.0 s**.
- `composite_over` blended the warp over the cleared layer in float buffers: **2.3 s**. When the warp box holds the whole layer, there is nothing under it to blend.

My claim comment said the mesh warp was 7–9× slower per pixel than Free Transform's. That was wrong for Flag: most of that time was these two steps.

### Change

- **`warp_cmds`:** `edit.transform.warp` (and `layer.smartObjects.warp`, which shares `apply`) runs its edit through `edit_job`, as Free Transform does since #4218. In the desktop app, a commit is a background job with progress, and Esc cancels it without touching the layer. Scripts, tests and the web build run inline as before.
  - `warp_layer` takes the job's `Interrupt`. It checks it between the steps that don't check it themselves.
  - A layer that already has alpha is cloned (its tiles are shared) instead of converted.
  - When clearing the warp box leaves the layer empty, the warp is the result, without `composite_over`. A test checks this gives the old path's pixels: exactly at 8 and 16 bits, and within one float ulp at 32 bits, where the old blend's `t·a / a` rounded a few values.
- **`algo::warp`:** `warp_mesh_surface_with` reports progress per destination tile and skips the remaining tiles once cancelled, like `warp_surface_with` (#4218). `warp_mesh_surface` and `warp_triangles` keep their signatures.
- **`transform_tool`:** Undo or Redo while a Warp commit runs now says "Warp is still being applied", instead of naming Free Transform. Nothing else in the UI needed changing: #4218's commit path already handles a pending job from either command, keeps the session's preview on screen and ends it when the job does.

Not in this PR: the mesh warp's own per-pixel speed. That's most of Arc's remaining 4.2 s, and it can now be cancelled. I'd look at it separately.

### Measured

8000 × 6000 RGBA8 layer filled with a pattern, engine level (`Session::execute` inline, `Session::start` for the job). Intel Core Ultra 7 255H (16 threads):

| | `main` | This PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Flag, inline | 9.3 s | **1.4 s** |
| Arc, inline | 6.9 s | **4.2 s** |
| UI thread blocked by a commit (job) | the whole warp | **0.2–1.1 ms** |
| Worker gone after cancel, 0.3 s / 1.5 s in | (no cancel) | Arc 31 / 66 ms, Flag 21 / 285 ms |

The 285 ms case is a cancel during the final write of the tiles, which doesn't check.

### Tests

- `algo`: `the_interruptible_mesh_warp_reports_progress_and_stops_when_cancelled`. Same pixels as `warp_mesh_surface`, progress above 0.9, and `None` when cancelled.
- `engine`:
  - `warp_runs_as_a_job_with_the_inline_result`: label "Warp", one undo step, same pixels as inline.
  - `a_cancelled_warp_leaves_the_document_unchanged`: the snapshot is not replaced, no undo step.
  - `a_warp_box_holding_the_whole_layer_gives_what_compositing_over_the_cleared_layer_did`: at 8, 16 and 32 bits.
  - `a_cancelled_warp_stops_in_a_selected_linked_mask`: a fill layer with a linked mask and a selection, warped with a cancelled interrupt, returns `Cancelled` (it ran to completion before the fix).
- `ui-egui`:
  - `a_warp_commit_runs_in_the_background_and_keeps_its_preview`: the job is labelled Warp, the session stays open with Undo refused, then it ends in one "Warp" step.
  - `esc_cancels_a_background_warp_commit`: the layer's pixels are untouched and there's no undo step.

included.head: 7adba7b4bb2df7778f56ddf0bc5c2a1ddc65b476
included.title: Make the Pencil cursor outline the pixels its dab fills
included.body:
Fixes #5262.

From 4 px up, the Pencil cursor (and the Eraser's in Pencil mode) was a smooth circle inside the dab's whole-pixel square. An aliased dab paints a stair-stepped disc of whole pixels: 4 px fills 12 pixels, 5 px fills 21, 9 px fills 69. The circle cut through the edge pixels, so it didn't show which ones a click would change. It also ignored roundness and angle: a 9 px tip at 50 % roundness showed the circle over a 37-pixel ellipse, and a 2.6 px tip showed a 3×3 square over a 5-pixel plus. In a rotated view, the 1–3 px square and the Block-mode Eraser's square were drawn as an upright box between two of their turned corners.

Trace the dab with the renderer's own rasterizer (`outline::aliased_outline`, next to `tip_outline`) and draw the boundary of the pixels it fills, with the dark-outside, light-inside one-pixel lines the square used. The outline is traced once per brush change and cached like `brush_cursor`'s tip outline, then moved by whole pixels to the pointer's grid cell and mapped through the view, so it turns, flips and follows Pixel Aspect Ratio Correction. The Block-mode Eraser's square takes the same path, at every zoom.

The Pencil falls back to the tip's smooth outline from `brush_cursor` below 100 %, at 100 % when Pixel Aspect Ratio Correction makes a document pixel narrower than a physical one (a ratio below 1), for a tip too big to trace (round over 508 px, sampled over about 359 px), for a tip so ragged its outline has more than 16,384 corners, and for a tip that fills no pixel. Below 100 % that outline sits on the pointer, as an OS cursor bitmap where one can show it; the dab lands within half a physical pixel of the pointer there. From 100 % up it is painted where the dab lands, as the square's circle was; at 800 % the dab's centre can be 4 points either way from the pointer. Under 6 points across the cursor still adds the hotspot crosshair, on the pointer, as the old cursor did. Past the size cap the smooth outline is within a pixel of the stair-steps, and a tip over the cap is turned away before `BrushContext::new` builds a sampled tip's mip pyramid, which would only be thrown away.

Also:
- The line colours come from `Tokens::cursor_outline`, like the other brush cursors, so the light line's alpha is 235 instead of 230.
- Both outline caches, `pencil_cursor`'s and `brush_cursor`'s, now trace a stored tip again once the preset store loads its full bitmap. Stored tips compare equal whether loaded or not, so a cursor first drawn during loading kept the preview's outline until the brush changed.

This follows echelon's note on #2214: Photoshop paints a pixelated circle for a round Pencil tip (#1057), so the cursor should outline that circle.

Tests:
- `pencil_tests::the_pencil_cursor_outlines_the_pixels_its_dab_fills` drives the real canvas at 800 % and compares the pixel-grid edges the cursor strokes with the boundary of a real `paint.pencil` dab at the same point. Its 35 cases cover sizes 1–12 at two sub-pixel positions, 2.6 and 4.4 px, roundness 0.5 at 0° and 30°, a rotated and flipped view, and the Eraser in Pencil and Block mode. With the base `canvas.rs`, 28 of them fail.
- `a_real_click_paints_exactly_what_the_pencil_cursor_outlined` and two siblings click the canvas 62 times and check that each click changes exactly the pixels the cursor outlined just before, in one undo step. They cover an asymmetric sampled tip turned and flipped, a squashed tip on every quarter turn of the view, the Pencil- and Block-mode Eraser on an opaque layer, 2×, 1.5× and 1.25× displays, and Pixel Aspect Ratio Correction at 2 and 0.91. With the base `canvas.rs`, 34 of 37, 10 of 13 and (at 2×) 4 of 4 clicks fail.
- `outline::tests` (paint) compare the traced outline with one-point aliased strokes at 8, 16 and 32 bits and in every colour mode: a tip with a hole, a thin 45° tip whose pixels touch only at corners, Block squares, two asymmetric tips turned, squashed and flipped (1,512 dabs), a seeded fuzz of 600 brushes, 810 hostile but finite size, roundness and angle combinations, and the 508 px limit. NaN, infinite, negative and 5000 px sizes give one pixel or no outline, without a panic. `the_cap_is_checked_before_the_mipmaps_are_built` checks that the early cap check uses the box the context's `dab_rect` gives, for 1,458 brushes: round, sampled, unusable and stored tips (loaded or not), sizes around both limits and sizes the renderer bounds, with roundness, angle, flips and the Block square.
- `pencil_cursor::tests` check where the two lines land (on physical pixels at 1×, 1.5× and 2×, and either side of every corner on turned, mirrored and stretched views), the fallback below 100 % and its hotspot, the Block square from 1 % to 6,400 %, and the cache. `at_100_percent_the_outline_is_drawn_at_any_ui_scale` covers UI scales where the 100 % check fell just short, since `(1 / ppp) · ppp` is 0.99999994 in f32: ppp 0.85 (85 % on a 1× display), 1.7 (85 % on 2×) and 2.25 × 1.1. `from_100_percent_an_untraceable_tip_is_centred_on_its_dab` checks that a tip over the cap is drawn around the dab's centre for any pointer over the dab: round at 100 %, 300 % and 800 %, squashed and turned, and sampled.
- `a_stored_tip_is_traced_again_once_its_full_bitmap_loads` (in `pencil_cursor` and in `brush_cursor`), `below_100_percent_a_tiny_pencil_still_shows_its_hotspot`, `at_100_percent_the_outline_is_drawn_at_any_ui_scale` and `from_100_percent_an_untraceable_tip_is_centred_on_its_dab` fail without their fixes.

`square_cursor_sits_on_the_pixel_grid` and `the_cursor_is_round_exactly_when_the_pencil_dab_is` go with the helpers they tested (`pencil_cursor_rect`, `pencil_tip_is_round`).

### Validation

On 7adba7b4:
- `cargo test -p photocraft-paint --lib`: 113 passed.
- `cargo test -p photocraft-ui-egui --lib`: 2,939 passed, 13 ignored.
- `cargo clippy -p photocraft-paint -p photocraft-ui-egui --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt -p photocraft-paint -p photocraft-ui-egui -- --check`: clean.
- `cargo xtask layers`: OK, 30 crates, no violations. `cargo xtask wasm`: OK.
- An offscreen wgpu render (throwaway test) of the 3, 4, 9 and 40 px cursors over a real dab at 300–1600 %, plus a 50 % roundness tip at 30° and a 30° rotated, flipped view: the outline sits on the dab's pixel edges in each.
- Tracing one dab in a release build, medians of five runs, ranges over five sessions on a machine running other builds: a round tip takes 0.09–0.16 ms at 100 px and 1.8–2.7 ms at 508 px; a sampled tip with a 64 × 64 bitmap 0.3–0.5 ms at 100 px and 4.0–6.0 ms at 359 px. A sampled tip with a 2500 × 2500 bitmap takes 11.7–15.1 ms at 100 px, nearly all of it the mip pyramid `BrushContext::new` builds (11.6–15.2 ms on its own), which each stroke with that tip builds too; nothing keeps it between strokes. Without the early cap check, the same tip took as long at 400 and 700 px (11.3–15.0 ms) to give no outline; with it, under a microsecond. With a 1024 px cap, a 1020 px round tip took 8.3 ms and a 721 px sampled tip 17.1 ms (one run), longer than a 60 Hz frame, so the cap is 512.

Notes:
- From 100 % up the outline stays snapped to the pixel grid, as the square was, so it shows what a click paints. #1057 also asks for Photoshop's unsnapped cursor; this doesn't change that.
- The cursor shows the plain tip at full pressure. Shape Dynamics, Scattering, Texture and the Dual Brush aren't reflected, and neither is Brush Pose › Override Pressure: with Pressure for Size on (the default), a mouse click then paints that fraction of the size, so a 20 px tip at 50 % fills 80 pixels, not the 316 outlined. Otherwise a mouse click is at full pressure, so Pressure for Size alone doesn't change it (a pen's lighter press does), and Transfer changes how much a click paints, not which pixels. The Ctrl+Alt resize preview still draws a smooth circle.
- `scorecard/tools.toml` TOOL-213-1 ("square pixel-aligned cursor") and the cursor row in `docs/brush-parity.md`, which #4420 also edits, aren't updated here.

Prepared with Claude Code assistance for @jonathanwxh-cell (jonathnwxh).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

included.title: Keep Free Transform preview colors consistent with the canvas
included.body:
Related to #5416.

Free Transform uploads document-color pixels directly while the surrounding canvas applies document-to-monitor conversion. On upstream, an AdobeRGB-compatible opaque sample changes from the canvas's #9C592D to #8C5933 when the transform preview appears. The actual drawn-texture regression fails on the wide-gamut case while its sRGB identity control passes: [baseline run](https://github.com/jonathanwxh-cell/photocraft/actions/runs/38549665214).

Apply the existing canvas display conversion to final preview uploads, including warp, covering layers and styled composites. Raw mip pixels remain available to effects. Display-profile cache keys prevent stale uploads, previous-profile textures are released, and native conversion runs in bounded parallel chunks. Selection tint and standalone mask/channel/path previews retain their diagnostic colors.

Verification on `d5e84c6` ([cloud run](https://github.com/jonathanwxh-cell/photocraft/actions/runs/38557574898)); the four submitted Rust files match that tested source exactly:

- Full UI crate: 2,801 tests passed, 14 ignored. Explicit offscreen rendering and the ignored release probe were also run and passed.
- Formatting, strict all-target UI Clippy, dependency layering and WASM passed.
- Regression coverage includes profile conversion, warp, covering layers, alpha preservation, selection tint, styled 16-bit previews, raw effect inputs and display-cache invalidation.
- Quick layout benchmark completed; cross-machine baseline comparison was skipped and quick mode does not enforce full-size budgets.
- Release 24 MP probe: first Display P3 preparation **512.461 ms**, identity sRGB **0.007 ms**; 1,000 cached P3 picks **9.287 microseconds**, with no new uploads. This measures CPU preparation, not GPU completion. Initial conversion remains noticeable at full resolution; cached dragging avoids repeating it. Earlier serial conversion measured 1,084.811 ms on a different runner, so no exact speedup ratio is claimed.

Original synthetic swatches, simulated Display P3 output; these are **before/during/after the transform on the candidate**, not before/after-fix captures. All six sRGB/P3 screenshots were inspected; the final parallel version produced byte-identical PNGs. [Evidence and attribution](https://github.com/jonathanwxh-cell/photocraft/tree/bf3ec9da3ceb7b1afd3204d058e8d8e120bb22b5).

| Before transform | During transform | After commit |
|---|---|---|
| ![Before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jonathanwxh-cell/photocraft/bf3ec9da3ceb7b1afd3204d058e8d8e120bb22b5/display-p3-before.png) | ![During](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jonathanwxh-cell/photocraft/bf3ec9da3ceb7b1afd3204d058e8d8e120bb22b5/display-p3-during.png) | ![After](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jonathanwxh-cell/photocraft/bf3ec9da3ceb7b1afd3204d058e8d8e120bb22b5/display-p3-after.png) |

The reporter's original document/profile is unavailable, so this addresses a reproduced cause without claiming all saturation cases are fixed. Existing isolated-preview transparency/blend limitations remain; the screenshots establish opaque-swatch consistency, not physical monitor calibration or full transparent-composite parity.

included.head: e7e96c4b83b06adfbd4db2f5b19c94924539f880
included.title: fix(format): report a failed directory flush after a save instead of ignoring it
included.body:
Fixes #4968.

`atomic_write` and the directory-bundle writer renamed the new file into place, then discarded the result of flushing the directory (`let _ = fs.sync_dir(&dir)`). Until that flush succeeds, the rename may not survive a power loss or crash. Yet the save reported complete success. Callers act on that success, so the risk was real:
- the document is marked saved;
- its crash-recovery entry is discarded;
- a bundle save goes on to remove the objects only the old manifest referenced.

The directory flush is real on Unix only (it's a no-op on Windows), so this affects Linux and macOS.

## Change

- **Flush failures are reported.** When the flush fails, `atomic_write` now returns an error. It keeps the error's kind and says the file was written but the save may not survive a power loss or crash. The caller then treats it as a failed save: the document stays unsaved, its recovery data stays, and the user can save again or elsewhere.
- **Bundle saves stop early.** The bundle writer (`write_bundle_file`) does the same. A failed flush after writing the manifest now stops the save before it removes unreferenced objects.
- **Unsupported flushes still count as saved.** A file system that can't flush directories at all still saves normally (`dir_synced`). That means EINVAL (some Linux file systems), ENOTSUP or EOPNOTSUPP, ENOTTY on Apple platforms, or `ErrorKind::Unsupported`. Retrying won't change those, and failing every save there would make saving impossible.

A folder that can't be opened for the flush at all, because it has write and search permission but no read permission, also counts as saved (`open_dir_for_sync`). No flush can be attempted there, and the existing permission tests save into such folders.

The errno values are spelled out per OS, as the existing Apple full-flush fallback already does, so no Unix-only API is needed.

## Tests

- `a_failed_directory_flush_is_reported_not_swallowed` injects a failing `sync_dir` through `AtomicFs`. The save returns an error of the same kind whose message names the file and says it may not survive. The new bytes are in place and no temporary file is left.
- `a_directory_flush_the_file_system_cannot_do_still_saves`:
  - an `Unsupported` flush still saves;
  - EINVAL counts as unsupported on Unix only;
  - EIO is an error.

The bundle writer's flush runs on Unix only, and this machine is Windows, so it has no test of its own here. It reuses `dir_synced` and returns before cleanup, which the format tests cover on every platform.

## Evidence

`387be71e` was checked in a clean checkout on Windows x86_64 (rustc 1.99.0), on `main` at the time:
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo xtask layers` and `cargo xtask wasm` pass.
- Workspace tests: 8,371 passed, 0 failed. The `marquee_autoscroll` wgpu binary crashed under parallel load, as it does on my machine, and passes on its own (3 tests).
- Workspace clippy first stopped because the disk was low. After I freed space, in the same checkout, workspace clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo xtask scorecard --check` and `git diff --check` pass.

included.title: fix(gpu): catch validation errors in watched compositor work
included.body:
The scoped_work function skipped error scopes when watched is true (always the case in the app because the canvas sets up health monitoring). But error scopes are needed on native platforms to catch synchronous validation errors (e.g. invalid buffer in queue.write_buffer). The health callbacks only handle device loss and async errors.

This fixes P12 (arrow-key nudge in a 150-layer document) which crashed with: wgpu error: Validation Error / Caused by: / In Queue::write_buffer / Buffer with pc_compose_uniforms label is invalid

Now scoped_work always uses error scopes on native (non-WASM) to catch validation/internal/OOM errors, while WebGPU relies on health callbacks for async errors.

included.head: 9902522df628167b2b0afdc987ab9d929ad125db
included.title: --version: name the commit of a dev build from git (#5247)
included.body:
Fixes #5247

A plain `cargo build` from `main` reported `photocraft --version` as `0.8.2 (dev build)`, which doesn't say which commit a bug report is about. It now reports `0.8.2 (dev build, 6f8505421)`.

**How:**
- `apps/photocraft/git_checkout.rs` is a build-script helper shared by the desktop and CLI `build.rs`. It runs `git rev-parse HEAD` and emits `PHOTOCRAFT_CHECKOUT_SHA`, and it asks for a rerun when `HEAD` or the current branch's ref changes (so on a commit or checkout). This works in worktrees as well.
- At startup the binaries pass that value to the new `build_info::set_checkout`. `long_version()` uses it only when `PHOTOCRAFT_BUILD_SHA` is unset.
- The engine still doesn't shell out to git (the existing design note in `build_info.rs`). The value lives in the two app crates, so a new commit rebuilds only those and not the engine and everything above it. I checked: after an empty commit, only `photocraft-cli` recompiled (17 s), and `--version` showed the new hash.

**Release logic unchanged:** when `PHOTOCRAFT_BUILD_SHA` is set (CI, `packaging/`, Docker), the build script does nothing and the output stays `0.8.2 (<sha>, <date>)`.

**Fallbacks:** with no git, no checkout, or a workspace that isn't the root of the repository it sits in (for example a source tarball unpacked inside another repo), nothing is set and the output stays `(dev build)`.

`docs/releasing.md` now mentions the dev-build format. Unit tests are in `build_info::tests::long_version_formats`.

Checks run locally, on this branch and on a merge of this branch with my other fixes from today (#5241–#5247):
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo xtask layers`

- `cargo test -p photocraft-engine --test panic_hunt -- --ignored`

Not run locally: `cargo xtask wasm` (this Gentoo toolchain has no wasm32 std), so CI has to check that. I also didn't run the full `cargo test --workspace`; the packages above are the ones this change touches.

included.head: 5e57be89cf66338222408f92f5ab7b7e31f2c1aa
included.title: docs(perf): how to measure one scenario and read its numbers
included.body:
The performance section explained how to run the whole benchmark, how to add a scenario and what CI
does — but not how to measure **one** scenario, nor the traps in reading the numbers. This adds both
to `docs/development.md` §"Scorecard and performance budgets":

- `xtask perf`'s exact flags, and the fact that it has **no `--only`**: to time one row you run the
  bench binary itself (`--only` matches row names with `contains`, plus `--group` and `--reps`),
  which writes its own report and does **not** evaluate budgets.
- `--reps` defaults to 7 in `--quick` and 15 otherwise, is per bench, and some rows cap it
  themselves (the `#211` algorithm rows use `b.reps.min(5)`). Percentiles are nearest-rank, so
  **at n ≤ 5 the "p95" is simply the maximum**.
- A budgeted scenario the baseline has no row for **fails** the run (`missing` is in
  `Status::fails()`), so the `[[scenario]]` and its baseline row belong together.
- A red `cargo xtask perf` is not necessarily your budget: the committed baseline carries

included.head: a75039792e05eb1839b0da2c628a8b73e95802a9
included.title: PSD Duotone: read and write the ink block (names, colours, curves)
included.body:
Follow-up to #4814, **on top of #4816**: until that PR is merged, this PR's diff includes its commits. The new work is the last commit.

PhotoCraft can now read and write the Duotone ink block (the PSD's Color Mode Data in Duotone mode).
- Opened duotones show their inks, not just the grey plate.
- Duotones made in PhotoCraft are saved as Duotone too. Before, they were saved as Grayscale with a warning.

## The block

The PSD specification leaves it undocumented. Photoshop 2025 writes 524 bytes; I made monotone, duotone, tritone and quadtone files with known inks in Photoshop and read the layout from them:

| offset | size | content |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 | version, 1 |
| 2 | 2 | ink count, 1–4 |
| 4 | 4 × 10 | ink colours, as in swatch files (`AcoColor`); space 0xFFFF = no ink |
| 44 | 4 × 64 | ink names, Pascal strings |
| 300 | 4 × 28 | curves: 13 × i16 then an i16 0, the PSD's transfer-function layout |
| 412 | 2 | dot gain, 20 |
| 414 | 11 × 10 | overprint colours, 0xFFFF = computed |

A curve's 13 values are the ink density in tenths of a percent at gray densities of 0, 5, 10, 20, …, 90, 95 and 100 %, and −1 leaves a point out. I checked the positions in Photoshop. PhotoCraft wrote a black monotone whose curve is 0 up to 60 % density and 100 % at 100 %, and Photoshop, after converting it to RGB, keeps it white exactly up to 60.4 % density.

## Changes

- **`duotone_map.rs` (new):**
  - `parse` reads the inks: RGB, CMYK, Lab and gray colours shown in sRGB, plus names and curves.
  - `write` makes the block from `Duotone::inks`. It writes RGB colours. A curve whose points lie on the 13-point grid keeps exactly those points; any other curve is sampled at all 13. It also writes the default dot gain and computed overprints.
- **Import:** interprets the inks. A colour-book ink can't be shown here, so it shows as black with a warning. The block is still kept raw (`psd_raw`) and written back unchanged while the inks are unedited, as before.
- **Export:** a Duotone without a raw block gets one from `write`, so every 8/16-bit Duotone is written as Duotone.

Photoshop's own conversion of a duotone to RGB uses dot gain and overprint colours that PhotoCraft's preview doesn't model yet. Colours on screen therefore differ from Photoshop's RGB conversion (by up to about 30 levels for a black and orange duotone with curves). That is the display model, not the file, and I've left it for later.

## Tests

- `duotone_map` unit tests:
  - The block for black and orange matches Photoshop's field by field.
  - Inks round-trip through write and parse, with on-grid, off-grid and plain curves.
  - Off-grid sampling is correct.
  - A colour-book ink reads as black with the flag set, and malformed blocks are refused.
- `a_duotone_made_in_photocraft_is_written_with_its_inks`: mode 8 with a 524-byte block, the inks read back with no duotone warning, and an unedited re-export writes the same block.
- `cargo test -p photocraft-io --features corpus` passes, and so do the `duotone` tests of `photocraft-engine`. clippy and fmt are clean.

included.head: 1b74873991dbb2e9803d228a969291f09c6f1032
included.title: Filter > Other > Frequency Separation (#1714)
included.body:
Closes #1714.

**Filter › Other › Frequency Separation…** sets up frequency separation in one step, instead of the duplicate / Gaussian Blur / Apply Image / blend mode routine.

From the active pixel layer it adds a **Frequency Separation** group right above it, holding:

- **Low Frequency** (Normal): the layer through Gaussian Blur at the chosen radius. These are the same pixels Filter › Blur › Gaussian Blur produces.
- **High Frequency** (Linear Light): `High = (Source − Low) / 2 + ½` in each colour channel, keeping the source's transparency.

This is Photoshop's recipe: Apply Image › Subtract, Scale 2, Offset 128 in 8-bit, and Add + Invert, Scale 2, Offset 0 in 16-bit, which give the same values. Linear Light computes `Low + 2·High − 1`, so the result is the source again. In 32-bit our Linear Light uses the same formula, so the recipe is unchanged there. The source layer itself is not modified, it is one history step, and the High layer ends up targeted, ready for healing.

The command is `layer.frequencySeparation` with `{"radius": 0.1..1000 = 4}`. From the menu it opens the existing schema dialog, which has a single Radius field. Photoshop has no menu item for this (people record it as an action), so the id is our own. The menu entry goes after Color to Alpha (`PLACE_AFTER`). I kept it out of `filter.*` because it adds layers rather than filtering the target, so mask/channel routing, Fade and Last Filter would all be wrong for it. The menu label is in all 17 catalogs, which the coverage test requires.

**Limits**

- Only RGB and Grayscale. In CMYK and Lab the compositor does not blend on the stored values (in a test the rebuild was off by 0.7 and 0.14), so the command is refused there rather than giving a wrong split.
- Linear Light clips to 0..1, so 32-bit values above 1 come back as 1.
- 8-bit stores High to the nearest level, so the rebuild is within ±1 level, the same as Photoshop's recipe.
- The new layers carry only the source's pixels (no mask, style, opacity or blending options), and the selection is ignored. The rebuild is exact for an opaque, Normal, 100% layer, which is the normal case for this technique.
- It is refused, with a message, on non-pixel layers (type, shape, adjustment, group, smart object), on empty layers, and when a channel, Quick Mask or layer mask is targeted.

Validation:
- Engine tests in the module: the composite of Low + High with the source hidden matches the source at 8/16/32-bit RGB and 8/32-bit Gray (tolerance 1/255, 1/65535, 1e-5); Low equals Gaussian Blur at radii 2 and 6.5; group/layer names, order, blend modes and the targeted layer; High's bounds equal the source's; one undo restores the document exactly and redo brings the result back; works on the Background; refusals listed above; bad params give `BadParams` and leave the document unchanged.
- Each new test was checked against a mutation that should break it: High without `/2`, mask/mask-view/colour-mode checks removed, Linear Light left out, radius ignored, empty-layer check removed. All of them failed.
- `cargo test -p photocraft-engine --test panic_hunt -- --ignored` passes.
- ui-egui: `menus::`, `filter_dialog::` and `i18n::` tests pass, including a new one for the menu position and dialog.
- `cargo clippy -p photocraft-engine -p photocraft-ui-egui --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo xtask layers`, `cargo xtask wasm` all pass. `cargo xtask parity` leaves the checklist unchanged.
- Checked rendered with the offscreen `snapshot` example: the Layers panel after the command, and the Radius dialog. (macOS, Apple silicon)
- Full `cargo test -p photocraft-ui-egui`: `new_doc_ui::tests::new_document_depth_labels_and_tooltips_are_translated` and `prefs_ui::tests::preference_labels_are_translated` fail the same way on `main`

included.head: c99df31a13a45536590e15c14208ea10f1f671d1
included.title: SVG import: set text in an installed font when the named ones are missing
included.body:
## Problem

On a Linux system without Windows fonts, text in an imported SVG is dropped. For example, Fedora 44 has neither Arial nor DejaVu Sans. The import then only warns "SVG: nothing to draw (an empty drawing)", although hundreds of fonts are installed. Because of this, `crates/io/tests/svg.rs` `text_becomes_outline_shapes_or_warns_without_a_font` fails on Fedora 44 on `main`.

## Cause

The SVG importer shapes text with its own `usvg::fontdb` database (`svg.rs` `fonts()`), not with the Fontconfig path of `photocraft-text` (#2961). fontdb does not know Fontconfig's aliases, and it maps the generic families to Windows fonts: `sans-serif` to Arial, `serif` to Times New Roman, `monospace` to Courier New.

So on such a system every family of a usual `font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif"` misses, including the generic one, and so does the `serif` default that usvg appends. usvg then drops the text chunk while parsing.

The warning from #3168 only fires when the font database is empty, so here the user just gets "nothing to draw".

```
$ fc-match 'DejaVu Sans'; fc-match Arial; fc-match sans-serif
NotoSans-Regular.ttf: "Noto Sans" "Regular"
LiberationSans-Regular.ttf: "Liberation Sans" "Regular"
NotoSans-Regular.ttf: "Noto Sans" "Regular"
```

Official builds are affected too: the bundled craft fonts are in the database, but no generic family points at them.

## Fix

`resolve_generic_families` points each generic family at a font the database holds, the way a browser falls back. In order of preference:

1. the system's choice, when the database has it (`fc-match <generic>` on Linux native; nothing elsewhere);
2. the first installed stand-in:
   - Liberation and Croscore, which are metric-compatible;
   - DejaVu and Noto;
   - the bundled Inter or JetBrains Mono;
3. the sans-serif choice;
4. any installed font.

A generic whose font is already installed is left alone, so systems with Arial and friends behave as before. `fc-match` runs at most once per process, when the font database is first loaded, which already only happens for drawings with text.

## Tests

- `text_in_missing_fonts_falls_back_to_an_installed_one`: the database holds only the bundled `assets/fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf`, with no system fonts and no Fontconfig. `Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif`, `Times New Roman`, `Courier New, monospace`, `cursive` and `fantasy` all produce the text layer. Without the fix it fails with the same "nothing to draw".
- `generic_families_point_at_installed_fonts`:
  - every generic resolves to an installed font;
  - the system's choice wins when installed;
  - an installed generic stays;
  - an empty database is left alone.
- `crates/io/tests/svg.rs` now passes on Fedora 44 (16/16). Checked by hand with `photocraft-cli convert` on an SVG with `Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif` and `Times New Roman, serif` text: both come out as type layers, in Noto Sans and Noto Serif.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo clippy -p photocraft-io --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p photocraft-io --lib --tests`: 487 passed, after a rebase on `main`.
- Before the rebase: `cargo test --no-fail-fast -p photocraft-io -p photocraft-engine -p photocraft-cli --lib --tests`.
  - All pass except `photocraft-cli` `missing_font_warning_tests::missing_typeface_is_reported_by_run_info_and_convert` (the missing-font warning is printed twice).
  - That test fails identically on `main` at `2aa1f8d2`, and passed at `476f9838`. It is unrelated to this change, and I can look into it separately.
- `cargo xtask layers`, `cargo xtask wasm`
- Corpus (`cargo test --release --no-fail-fast --features corpus,heif` on psd, codecs, io and engine): all pass.

included.head: 055681bf83c127405c044077a2b52a4e6bbd282d
included.title: Security: pin and verify the Windows signing client (#2936)
included.body:
## Summary

`packaging/windows/sign.ps1` downloaded `Microsoft.Trusted.Signing.Client` from the unversioned NuGet URL and loaded its dlib into `signtool`, next to the Azure signing secrets, with no version or integrity check (#2936, finding 1 of #1372). Once #3794 passes the Azure secrets to the release workflow, this branch is what PhotoCraft's own Windows releases will run.

The script now downloads a pinned version (1.0.95) and checks its SHA-256 before extracting it. On a mismatch it throws and never runs `signtool`. Upgrading the client is now a deliberate change to both values, and the comment above them says how to make it.

## No change to what gets signed today

- The unversioned URL resolves to 1.0.95 today (it redirects to `microsoft.trusted.signing.client.1.0.95.nupkg`). I downloaded it and the versioned URL, and the two files are byte-identical: SHA-256 `3bfcf1e0a3cb42af1692f0a8ed45c15de070c2de86f28a59b2795d904d8a920f`.
- NuGet's catalog entry for 1.0.95 lists the same SHA-512 and size (14,651,525 bytes).
- The package's `.signature.p7s` names Microsoft Corporation as the author signer, countersigned by the NuGet.org repository. I decoded it but did not validate the certificate chain.
- nuget.org keeps the existing signatures on published packages when it rotates its repository certificate ([NuGet blog, March 2024](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/nuget/the-nuget-org-repository-signing-certificate-will-be-updated-as-soon-as-april-8th-2024/)), so the pinned bytes shouldn't change underneath us.

## Testing

`sign.ps1` has no automated test and real signing needs the release secrets. I ran the Azure branch on Windows 11 under PowerShell 7.6 (the release workflow's `pwsh`) with dummy `AZURE_*` values and `SIGNTOOL` pointing at a stub. The stub logs its arguments and exits 1, the way signtool fails on dummy credentials.

- **Pinned version, expected hash:** the script downloads 1.0.95, the hash matches, and it passes `client\bin\x64\Azure.CodeSigning.Dlib.dll` to `signtool sign … /dlib … /dmdf …`. It then stops with "signtool sign failed with exit code 1", as expected with dummy credentials.
- **Expected hash altered by one byte:** the script stops with `Microsoft.Trusted.Signing.Client 1.0.95 has SHA-256 3BFC…920F, expected 00FC…920F: refusing to load it`. `signtool` is never called.
- The temporary `photocraft-sign-*` folder is removed in both runs.
- The packaging-lint PowerShell step (`Parser::ParseFile` on `packaging/windows/*.ps1`, then `check-icons.ps1`) passes locally.

No Rust code changes.

## Docs

- `docs/releasing.md`: the Signing section says the client is pinned and where the pin lives.
- `book/src/development/release-security.md`: the pin is listed under implemented elements.

## Note for a follow-up

Every version of `Microsoft.Trusted.Signing.Client` is now unlisted on NuGet. Microsoft renamed Trusted Signing to Artifact Signing and asks existing customers to update their client tools ([Artifact Signing](https://azure.microsoft.com/products/artifact-signing)). The successor package is [`Microsoft.ArtifactSigning.Client`](https://www.nuget.org/packages/microsoft.artifactsigning.client).

This PR keeps today's package and only pins it. Moving to the successor changes the signing toolchain, so it belongs in its own change that can be tested against the real Azure account. The same pin applies to it.

Fixes #2936

included.head: 92488307722c3b840507827cac7ee9a88470fc8a
included.title: fix(layer-style): support Blend If Alt-split handle feathering and throttle live preview
included.body:
### Summary
1. Fixes Blend If slider handle interaction: Alt-dragging a black or white triangle now splits it into two half-handles (`[min, max]`) for smooth feathered luminance blending, matching Photoshop 1:1.
2. Resolves heavy CPU spikes and stuttering during slider drag by throttling live Layer Style document preview compositing to ~30 FPS on the UI thread.

### Details
- **Alt-Split Triangle Handles:** Refactored slider drag math in `blend_if_bar` (`layer_style.rs`). Alt-dragging the black triangle splits the right half (`[0, max]`); Alt-dragging the white triangle splits the left half (`[min, 255]`). Dragging halves back together seamlessly reunites them. Handle ordering `0 <= black_lo <= black_hi <= white_lo <= white_hi <= 255` is strictly maintained.
- **Live Preview CPU Throttling:** In `canvas.rs`, dragging sliders previously triggered full synchronous CPU composite passes on every pointer move event (up to 120+ times/sec), pegging CPU cores at 100%. Live Layer Style preview rendering is now throttled to ~30 FPS (>= 33ms) during rapid drag gestures, while guaranteeing the final state is always rendered immediately upon release or timer trigger.

included.head: 3a85e5a674375ec44ba7c77a41147c5183af24b2
included.title: Open GIMP XCF files: layers, groups, masks, blend modes, channels and selection
included.body:
Closes #1076.

## What changed

PhotoCraft opens **GIMP XCF** files (`.xcf`, `.xcf.gz`), read only, through a new reader in `photocraft-io` (`crates/io/src/xcf.rs`, about 1,000 lines) written from the [public XCF specification](https://developer.gimp.org/core/standards/xcf/) and from files GIMP 3.2 writes; no GIMP code. Save suggests `.pcraft`; exporting as `.xcf` fails with a message, as PDN does.

- **Read:** XCF versions 0 to 26 (32-bit pointers up to 10, 64-bit after; newer files open with a note); uncompressed, RLE and zlib tiles; 8/16/32-bit integer and 16/32/64-bit float precisions (32-bit integer opens as 16-bit, floats as 32-bit float with HDR values kept; linear-light precisions get a linear sRGB or linear gray profile); RGB and grayscale as such, indexed through its colour map as RGB.
- **Layers:** any size and position (off-canvas too), opaque layers as locked-transparency layers, groups rebuilt from `PROP_ITEM_PATH` (nested, Pass through), names, opacity (`FLOAT_OPACITY` over `OPACITY`), visibility, offsets, layer masks applied or disabled, lock alpha/content/position, colour tags, GIMPhoto's `gimphoto-clipped` parasite as a clipping mask.
- **Blend modes:** the 2.10 set and the legacy set mapped to Photoshop's; Addition → Linear Dodge, Dodge/Burn → Color Dodge/Burn, HSV/LCH/luma modes to the HSL-based ones with a note, and the seven with no counterpart (Behind, Grain extract/merge, Color erase, Erase, Merge, Split) as Normal with a note naming the layer.
- **Image:** ICC profile (`icc-profile` parasite), resolution, guides, the comment (as document text metadata), extra channels as alpha channels, the saved selection as the selection.
- **Reported, not applied:** GIMP 3 layer effects (the layer opens unfiltered), paths, floating selections; text, vector and link layers open as their pixels.
- **Never panics:** every read is bounds-checked; canvases ≤ 300,000 px a side and 1 GiB of pixels, ≤ 8,192 layers, ≤ 1,024 channels, nesting ≤ 64, payloads ≤ 64 MiB, gzip inflation ≤ 1 GiB; tile data decoded to the exact declared size; the property lengths the spec warns about (`PROP_COLORMAP`, `PROP_USER_UNIT`) are computed, not trusted; cancellation checked per layer and per 64 tiles.
- **Wiring:** `IoError::Xcf`, detection by the `gimp xcf ` signature or the extension, `xcf` in File › Open, the batch commands and the web app; `docs/xcf.md`, the file-format parity table, the README Formats paragraph, `ATTRIBUTION.md`.

### How the composite differs from GIMP (documented in `docs/xcf.md`, each noted on open)

Three GIMP defaults have no Photoshop counterpart; the tests measure each:
- GIMP blends most modes and composites every layer in **linear light**; PhotoCraft (like Photoshop) in the document's encoding. A layer set to *RGB (perceptual)* in GIMP matches within 2.5/255 (the tolerance the tests enforce).
- Every mode but Normal composites with **Clip to backdrop**: the layer shows nothing where the layers beneath are transparent.
- For modes whose result can leave 0..1 (Addition, Subtract, Divide, Dodge, Burn, Linear light) GIMP **clamps after** applying the pixel's alpha; Photoshop before. Opaque pixels match exactly.

## Screenshots

Rendered offscreen with the `snapshot` example.

| *The Great Wave off Kanagawa* (Hokusai; public domain) saved by GIMP 3.2 as an XCF with a text layer, a group holding a 65% Multiply tint with a half-black mask, and guides, opened in PhotoCraft | GIMP's `groups.xcf` fixture at 1600%: nested groups, a pass-through group, offsets |
|---|---|
| ![demo xcf open](https://github.com/diegochagas/photocraft/blob/assets/xcf-read/xcf-open.png?raw=true) | ![groups fixture](https://github.com/diegochagas/photocraft/blob/assets/xcf-read/xcf-groups.png?raw=true) |

The 16-bit grayscale fixture opens as `Gray/16`:

![gray16 fixture](https://github.com/diegochagas/photocraft/blob/assets/xcf-read/xcf-gray16.png?raw=true)

## How it was tested

- **Unit tests** (`crates/io/src/xcf/tests.rs`, 15): a small XCF writer built from the specification produces files for every compression (none, RLE, zlib), 16-bit and 16/32/64-bit float samples (big-endian), version 0 and 3 (32-bit pointers, legacy modes), properties (offsets, opacity, mode, visibility, locks, tags), groups by item path with pass-through and a path that leads nowhere, masks applied or not at the layer offset, indexed colour maps, extra channels and the selection, resolution/guides/comment/ICC parasites and unknown properties, clipping/text/vector/floating-selection reporting, RLE long runs and literals, limits and malformed structures, gzipped files, and every truncation of a file (never a panic).
- **GIMP-written fixtures** (`crates/io/tests/xcf.rs`, 13 tests; `cargo test -p photocraft-io --test xcf`): nine files written by GIMP 3.2.6 itself (`scripts/xcf_fixtures.py`, run inside GIMP) from procedural images the tests regenerate, plus `-perceptual` variants of five of them with every layer set to blend and composite in gamma-encoded RGB, each with GIMP's merged rendering as a PNG (28 files, 251 KB). Layer data is checked sample for sample (8-bit RGB/RGBA, 16-bit gray and gray+alpha, 32-bit float with values above 1, masks, offsets including off-canvas, opacity, modes, visibility, locks, tags, resolution, guides, groups and nesting, channels and the selection, indexed colour, a text layer). Our composite against GIMP's:
  - `layers-8bit-perceptual`, `mask-perceptual`, `text-perceptual`: within **2.5/255** everywhere; `gray16`, `indexed`, `channel`: within 2/255.
  - `groups-perceptual`: within 2.5/255 except the 15% of pixels where GIMP's Clip to backdrop hides the Multiply/Screen children above the transparent part of the background.
  - `legacy-modes-perceptual`, per mode: Addition, Subtract, Divide, Dodge, Burn, Hard light, Exclusion and Linear light within **2.5/255 on opaque pixels**; the translucent pixels of the unbounded ones differ by GIMP's clamp-after-alpha (measured 28–125/255, explained in `docs/xcf.md`); Grain merge, HSV Hue/Value and LCH Color are the approximations and are reported.
  - GIMP's default (linear-light) files: the known gap, measured and pinned: 38/255 (Multiply at 60%), 59/255 (mask edge), 73/255 (text edge), 138/255 (groups over transparency).
- `cargo test -p photocraft-io --lib --tests`: every binary ok. `cargo clippy -p photocraft-io --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean (with the `as_chunks` form CI's clippy 1.99 asks for). `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean. `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p photocraft-io`: ok. `cargo xtask test-corpus -p io`: running when this PR was opened; its result follows as a comment.
- **Code review** (medium): 4 findings; 1 fixed (the linear-light note now covers every gamma precision, not only 8-bit), 3 left as follow-ups: GIMP's XMP/EXIF parasites are not imported yet, each drawable goes through a full-size f32 scratch buffer (bounded by the 1 GiB budget), and a damaged `PROP_USER_UNIT` fails the file instead of being skipped.
- Not done: GIMP's own `app/tests/files/gimp-2-6-file.xcf` (GPL) is not used; a local opt-in corpus of real-world XCFs would be the next step, as for PDN and Krita.

## Risk and rollback

Risk class: a new read-only importer; nothing existing changes behaviour (`.xcf` files were "unknown file format" before). Rollback: revert this PR.

  * Open XCF files through the web file picker and recognize them in batch file discovery.
* **Documentation**

included.head: 0bc83d18bba12a99a10c75d97e1e8d3cb8bde62f
included.title: select.cryptomatte: click an object, select its coverage
included.body:
The Cryptomatte picker on top of the merged #2180 codec — the Arnold/V-Ray/Redshift workflow: click an object in the render, get its exact selection.

**`select.cryptomatte {x, y, layer?, tolerance?, mode?}`**

- Reads the ID at the clicked pixel of the active document's **source EXR** (the Cryptomatte layer by name, default the first; the document must have been opened from a saved `.exr`, everything else says so).
- Builds the selection from every pixel that ID **covers** — partial coverage becomes a partial mask, so an edge falls between both objects instead of hard-cutting. `tolerance` groups near-identical IDs (default 0: exact).
- Returns the ID, the **manifest's object name**, the pixel count and the layer used — the name is what a status-bar line or MCP caller shows.
- `mode` replace/add/subtract/intersect combines like the marquee tools; clicking a pixel with no samples deselects in replace mode (Magic Wand behaviour).

Everything is a command, so the control channel, CLI and MCP drive the same selection headlessly; the UI picker panel can follow as a thin shell.

**Tests** (synthetic 4×4 file: `cube` at coverage 1 on the left half, `sphere` at 0.5 on the right, manifest naming both): exact pixels and name for a full-coverage click, 0.5 mask at the half-covered pixel, add/subtract arithmetic (0.5 − 0.5 → 0.25), layer-by-name, and a hostile-param sweep (missing, non-numeric and out-of-bounds coordinates, unknown layer and mode — all `Err`, never a panic). `panic_hunt` green; engine suite 1161 green; clippy/fmt clean.

## Summary

Addresses #2301.

Extend PhotoCraft's existing toolbar flyout interaction
to support dragging from a grouped tool button into its
flyout and releasing over the desired tool.

## Problem

Grouped tools already support right-click and long-press
flyouts.

However, dragging away from the original button does not
provide the complete Photoshop-style press-drag-release
selection workflow.

## Changes

- Detect dragging away from a grouped tool button.
- Open the corresponding tool flyout during that gesture.
- Allow releasing the primary pointer over a flyout item
  to select that tool.
- Prevent the original toolbar button from activating
  after the flyout gesture.
- Preserve existing right-click and long-press behavior.
- Add regression tests for drag opening and release targets.

## Expected Behavior

1. Press a grouped toolbar tool.
2. Drag away from the button.
3. The grouped tool flyout appears.
4. Move over another tool.
5. Release to select that tool.

## Validation

Implementation and regression test committed.
Native pointer interaction and Rust tests remain pending.

included.title: Scroll the viewport while outlining with Polygonal Lasso
included.body: Polygonal Lasso now scrolls the canvas while the pointer rests near or just past an active viewport edge, including between vertex clicks with the button released. This lets a zoomed-in outline continue into an offscreen area without manually switching to navigation. Fixes #2231. Scrolling keeps placed vertices in document coordinates, uses the existing rotated, mirrored and pixel-aspect-aware view mapping and Overscroll bounds, and requests further frames for a stationary pointer. Returning to the interior, opening a dialog or using temporary navigation stops automatic motion. An unfinished polygon is tied to its starting document so switching documents or tools cannot later commit it to a different document. Shift-constrained segments remain supported while the view scrolls. included.title: feat(actions): import and export reusable Actions JSON files
included.body:
## Summary

Partially addresses #1951.

PhotoCraft persists recorded actions internally, but users
cannot conveniently export their action libraries or import
actions from another installation.

This adds JSON import/export through the engine commands `actions.import` and `actions.export`, using PhotoCraft's existing versioned ActionsFile format. The Actions panel, CLI, and MCP share the engine implementation.

## Changes

### Actions Panel

Add an Actions menu containing:

- Load Actions… (supports JSON alongside the existing ATN path)
- Save Actions… (.json)

The panel keeps file selection and status messages; merge, rename, validation, nested-reference retargeting, and serialization run in the engine. Menu labels and status strings are translated.

### Export

- Export the current action library as JSON.
- Use the existing ActionsFile version 1 format.
- Preserve action names, commands, parameters, and order.
- Enforce the existing 16 MiB Actions file limit.
- Report successful exports through the status system.

### Import

- Read versioned Actions JSON files.
- Preserve existing actions.
- Append new actions to the library.
- Skip already imported identical actions.
- Rename conflicting imports using `(Imported N)`.
- Retarget nested action references after renaming.
- Support nested references by action name or imported index.
- Update the action-library revision for persistence.
- Prevent imports while actions are recording or playing.

### File Validation

Reject:

- Invalid JSON.
- Unsupported file versions.
- Files exceeding the 16 MiB limit.
- Empty or duplicate action names.
- Excessively long action names.
- More than 1,024 imported actions.
- More than 10,000 steps per action.
- Invalid nested action indexes.

### Regression Tests

Added tests for:

- Export/import round-trip preservation.
- Repeated imports without creating duplicates.
- Duplicate-name handling.
- Nested action reference preservation.
- Invalid JSON and unsupported versions.
- Duplicate action names.
- Import rejection during recording.
- Existing action preservation after failed imports.

## Compatibility

This uses PhotoCraft's native JSON Actions format.

It does not add Photoshop `.atn` import support.

## Files Changed

- crates/ui-egui/src/actions.rs

## Validation

Completed:
- Four commits pushed to an isolated branch.
- Source-level implementation review.
- Regression tests added.
- Remote branch verification.
- Duplicate contribution screening.

Pending:
- cargo fmt --all -- --check
- cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
- cargo test -p photocraft-ui-egui
- Native file picker verification
- Browser import/export verification
- Persistence regression testing
- Upstream CI

Tests have not been executed.

## Issue

Partially addresses #1951.

The Play-button behavior is handled in a separate PR.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Import and export actions as portable JSON files, while retaining support for existing `.atn` files.
  * Imported actions are added without duplicating equivalent actions; name conflicts are resolved automatically, and nested action references are preserved.
  * After importing, the matching action is selected and expanded. JSON exports include disabled steps, dialog settings, and action sets.
  * A “Save Actions…” option lets you export your actions to a JSON file.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Path-based `actions.export` requests are rejected when ambient filesystem access is not allowed.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

At `202266b9`, five focused JSON engine tests and the adversarial command panic-hunt test passed locally. Hosted Linux/Windows tests, formatting, Clippy, corpus, wasm, and web checks passed. The color-metadata deduplication regression covers renamed import and idempotent repeat import.
